banking.summary: A bank makes money by lending it out and by moving it around. So most of what can go wrong sits in those two places: loans that never get paid back, and payments that end up with the wrong person. Banks are also legally required to spot money laundering and fraud, and regulators check they are holding enough money to survive a bad year.
hallmarks: Loans get approved because the customer is important, not because the numbers work
Checks for money laundering get rushed or skipped, which is a legal problem, not just a lost-money problem
The bank guesses how customers will behave, and builds its safety buffers on those guesses
Customers get sold products that are wrong for them, and the bank has to pay them back later
banking.regulatory: Rules that apply here: Basel (how much money a bank must keep in reserve), anti-money-laundering law, consumer protection rules, and IFRS 9 / CECL (how a bank estimates the loans it will not get back).

insurance.summary: An insurer takes money now and promises to pay out later, so its accounts are built on estimates of what those payouts will cost. If the estimate is too low, the company looks more profitable than it is. Most of the rest of the risk sits in how claims are handled and how policies are sold.
hallmarks: The money set aside for future claims is an estimate, and estimates can be nudged to make results look better
Claims get paid for more than the policy actually requires, because nobody checks the wording closely
Reinsurance is meant to cover the big losses, but only works if it was set up properly beforehand
Brokers and agents sell in the insurer's name, so their mistakes become the insurer's problem
insurance.regulatory: Rules that apply here: solvency rules (how much capital an insurer must hold), IFRS 17 or local reserving rules, and conduct rules covering how policies are sold.

logistics.summary: A logistics business moves other people's goods, using vehicles and staff spread across a wide area. Margins are thin, so small losses matter. The main things that go wrong are deliveries that never get invoiced, fuel and vehicles that are hard to keep track of, goods that go missing in the network, and safety rules that stop the operation if broken.
hallmarks: Shipments get delivered but never invoiced, or invoiced at the wrong rate
Fuel is easy to take and hard to trace back to a specific vehicle or trip
Freight changes hands many times, and each handover is a chance to lose it
Driver hours, dangerous goods and customs rules — break these and the operation stops
logistics.regulatory: Rules that apply here: driver hours-of-service limits, dangerous goods handling rules, customs requirements, and IFRS 15 / ASC 606 (revenue is earned as the goods move, not when they leave).

aviation.summary: An airline or ground handler works under strict safety rules and owns or leases very expensive aircraft. Paperwork is not admin here — if maintenance records are incomplete, the aircraft cannot fly. On the money side, tickets are sold long before the flight happens, so what counts as revenue and what is still owed to the customer needs care.
hallmarks: Maintenance was done but the records do not prove it, so the aircraft is grounded anyway
A ticket sold is not revenue yet — it becomes revenue when the passenger actually flies
Leased aircraft must be handed back in a specific condition, and the cost of that is easy to underestimate
Aircraft get damaged on the ground, and it is not always clear who caused it
aviation.regulatory: Rules that apply here: airworthiness and maintenance regulations, ground handling standards, IFRS 16 (leases) and IFRS 15 (when ticket sales become revenue).

manufacturing.summary: A manufacturer buys materials, converts them into products, and holds a lot of stock along the way. Most of the risk is in whether the stock is really there, whether it is valued correctly, and whether the factory is running safely and within its environmental permits.
hallmarks: The cost used to value products is out of date, so profit margins are wrong
Material is wasted or scrapped, and the loss disappears into general variances
Stock shows on the system but is not on the shelf
Safety and environmental permits carry conditions that must be evidenced, not just claimed
manufacturing.regulatory: Rules that apply here: environmental permits and emissions reporting, workplace safety law, and product liability and warranty obligations.

retail.summary: A retailer handles a very large number of small transactions across many stores. No single sale matters much, which is exactly why losses build up unnoticed. The main risks are cash going missing at the till, stock disappearing between supplier and shelf, and money owed to customers through gift cards and loyalty points.
hallmarks: Staff process refunds or voids against real sales and take the cash
Stock goes missing through theft, mistakes and short deliveries, all mixed together
Money promised by suppliers is counted as profit before it has actually been earned
Gift cards and loyalty points are money owed to customers, and it is easy to understate it
retail.regulatory: Rules that apply here: consumer protection and pricing rules, card payment security standards (PCI DSS), and food safety rules where food is sold.

hospitality.summary: A hotel handles cash, food, drink and people at every property, while head office oversight is spread thin. Most losses are small and local: discounts given at the front desk, drink poured beyond the recipe, buying done outside the group's agreed suppliers.
hallmarks: Free or discounted rooms given at the front desk without anyone approving it
More drink is used than the sales suggest, and the gap is written off as waste
Hotels buy locally at higher prices, sometimes from suppliers connected to staff
Booking websites take a large commission, which can wipe out the profit on a room
hospitality.regulatory: Rules that apply here: food safety and licensing, card payment security standards, and employment rules covering tips and service charges.

ecommerce.summary: An online retailer is a business made of transactions and customer data. The money takes a path from the customer's card, through a payment provider, to the bank account — and it needs to be reconciled at each step. The other big exposure is personal data: what is held, how long, and who else gets to see it.
hallmarks: Orders taken, money collected by the payment provider, and cash in the bank do not match
Fraudulent orders get shipped, then the payment is reversed and the goods are gone
Refunds get issued without the goods ever coming back
Customer data is kept longer, and shared wider, than the law allows
ecommerce.regulatory: Rules that apply here: data protection and privacy law, card payment security standards, consumer rights on returns and refunds.

fmcg.summary: A consumer goods company sells through supermarkets and distributors, and spends heavily on promotions to get shelf space. That promotional spend is the biggest area of judgement. The other major risk is product safety — if something is wrong with a batch, the company has to be able to find and withdraw it quickly.
hallmarks: Money is committed to promotions without anyone checking whether they worked
Retailers deduct amounts from invoices, and those deductions get paid without being verified
Extra stock is pushed to distributors near period end to hit targets, and comes back later
If a batch has a problem, the company must be able to trace where it went — quickly
fmcg.regulatory: Rules that apply here: food safety systems (HACCP), labelling and advertising standards, and product recall obligations.

utilities.summary: A utility is usually a regulated monopoly running safety-critical equipment. Prices and service levels are set by a regulator, so compliance is not optional. The main risks are billing customers for the right amount of energy or water, keeping the network safe, and treating customers in difficulty properly.
hallmarks: Energy or water delivered does not match what gets billed, and the difference is guessed at
The licence contains conditions that must be evidenced, and often nobody owns them
Safety-critical maintenance is delayed to save money
Customers in hardship, or on medical equipment, get cut off when they should not be
utilities.regulatory: Rules that apply here: the operating licence and price controls set by the regulator, customer protection and hardship rules, and safety and environmental law.

telecom.summary: A telecoms company handles a huge number of calls, messages and data sessions, which pass through several systems before they turn into a bill. Records get lost along the way, and each lost record is money never charged. The network itself is the other big risk — when it goes down, it is a public and regulatory event.
hallmarks: Usage happens on the network but never reaches the billing system, so it is never charged
Services get switched on for customers who were never set up to be billed
Amounts owed by other operators are settled using their numbers, not the company's own
A badly controlled network change causes an outage that has to be reported to the regulator
telecom.regulatory: Rules that apply here: telecoms licence conditions, outage reporting duties, data retention and privacy rules, and consumer contract rules.
